Article.ArticleTitle: Case Report: Longitudinal clonal evolution in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma with coexisting MET exon 14 skipping and EML4-ALK fusion and subsequent KRAS/BRAF bypass mutations.

Abstract.AbstractText: Acquired resistance to osimertinib in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant non-small cell lung cancer occurs through on-target mutations or bypass activation of alternative pathways. The longitudinal molecular evolution of a tumor across successive lines of therapy is rarely captured by repeat biopsy. We report a 68-year-old never-smoking woman with EGFR exon 19 deletion lung adenocarcinoma. First-line therapy achieved a partial response, with progression after 10.7 months; after 61 months of osimertinib, re-biopsy revealed concurrent EGFR T790M (9.3%), EML4-ALK fusion (E6:A20; 6.0%), and MET exon 14 skipping (c.3028G>T; 4.0%); aumolertinib plus ensartinib achieved stable disease for approximately 13 months. On further progression, a third biopsy showed molecular changes consistent with clonal evolution: the EML4-ALK fusion, MET exon 14 alteration, and EGFR T790M were no longer detected; the EGFR exon 19 deletion expanded to 47.71%; and KRAS G12R (10.17%), KRAS L19F (7.85%), BRAF D594N (8.13%), and BRAF E501K (6.38%) had emerged. Treatment with ivonescimab, a programmed cell death protein 1 and vascular endothelial growth factor bispecific antibody, plus pemetrexed and carboplatin, followed by pemetrexed plus ivonescimab, achieved stable disease; because chemotherapy was given concurrently, the contribution of ivonescimab cannot be isolated. PD-L1 (tumor proportion score <1%) was assessed on an earlier biopsy and blood tumor mutational burden was measured in 2019. This case is consistent with longitudinal clonal dynamics under sequential targeted therapy, namely regression of drug-sensitive clones and emergence of mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway bypass alterations, and the feasibility of an immunotherapy-containing regimen in a multi-driver tumor with unfavorable immune biomarkers.

Article.ArticleTitle: Case Report: Long-term survival of a patient with lung adenocarcinoma harboring EGFR 19del/T790M/C797S and KIF26B-NTRK1 rearrangement.

Abstract.AbstractText: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) gene mutation stands as one of the most prevalent driver genetic alterations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). While targeted therapies against EGFR have substantially enhanced patient prognosis, acquired resistance remains a core challenge that limits therapeutic efficacy. Patients with stage IV NSCLC generally exhibit a dismal prognosis, with only about 7% of those with stage IVB disease surviving beyond five years. Herein, we report a case of a 47-year-old female patient diagnosed with advanced lung adenocarcinoma, whose clinical course has persisted for nearly a decade. Initial genetic testing identified an EGFR exon 19 deletion (19del). Following treatment with osimertinib, the patient developed concurrent cis-arranged EGFR T790M/C797S double mutations and a neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase 1 (NTRK1) gene rearrangement. Subsequently, through a multimodal therapeutic strategy integrating local intervention, radiation therapy, and targeted therapy, the patient's disease has been sustainably controlled for several years, and she remains alive with stable clinical status to date. NTRK1 fusions are a well-defined mechanism of acquired resistance to EGFR-TKIs, but they are uncommon. This case reports a KIF26B-NTRK1 rearrangement not previously described in lung cancer; however, its functional significance remains to be confirmed. The principal value of this report lies in the completeness of the longitudinal molecular and clinical record, which documents how an on-target mutation and a bypass rearrangement can coexist and persist.
